I am a 56-year-old woman who has farmed the same land in Quzhou County since I was a young bride. I never went to school, but I know every plot of my fields the way a mother knows her children. My family has six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. I do not gamble with strange crops — what has fed three generations will feed us again.

This year, like every year, I will plant **winter wheat** in early October and harvest it in early June, then immediately put in **summer maize** on the same land and harvest it before National Day. It is the rotation my neighbors and I have always followed. The wheat gives us grain for flour and a stable sale price, and the maize goes to the feed market. I would not dream of breaking this cycle — the soil knows it, and the buyers know it.

For seed, I will buy **improved wheat seed** (something like Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502) from the township seed station and **hybrid maize seed** (Deng Hai 605) from the dealer in town. I save my own wheat seed some years, but the new varieties yield better and resist disease, so I pay a little extra. The maize must be hybrid — everyone knows open-pollinated maize cannot compete anymore.

Before wheat sowing, I will run the **rotary tiller** over the fields to break up the stubble and level the ground. After the wheat comes off in June, I will **plant the maize with no tillage** — there is no time to waste, and the moisture will escape if I disturb the soil. My son helps me hire the seed drill from the village cooperative.

For fertilizer, I will spread about **100 kg per mu of compound fertilizer** (roughly 18-22-5 N-P₂O₅-K₂O) as a basal dressing for both crops. For the wheat, I will top-dress with urea once in the spring when it greens up, about **50 kg per mu**. For the maize, I will side-dress with urea at the jointing stage, about **40 kg per mu**. In total, that works out to roughly **20 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu** for the wheat, and **18 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu** for the maize. I do not do soil tests — I go by what my father taught me and what the extension agent says at the village meeting.

Irrigation comes from our well. The wheat needs water four times: the **winter irrigation** in December to protect from frost, and then three more times in spring at green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. The maize is tougher — two irrigations, one at the seedling stage if it is dry, and one at the big trumpet stage. That is what our electricity and water bills can afford.

For pests, I spray **three times** per crop: once for weeds with herbicide right after sowing, and twice for insects during the growing season. The wheat gets aphids some years, and the maize gets armyworm if we are unlucky. I buy the chemicals from the same shop in the county town every year.

If the weather is normal and no disaster comes, I expect about **1,050 kg of wheat per mu** and **1,150 kg of maize per mu**. Some of the wheat we keep for our own flour; the rest, along with all the maize, we sell to the grain merchant who drives to the village. It is not a rich life, but it is steady, and I know it by heart.
